title: How Modern AI Works: A No-Math Mental Model for PMs
monthTitle: AI Literacy and LLM Foundations for PMs
summary: A no-math mental model of how modern AI works—machine learning, neural networks, and generative AI—so PMs can reason confidently about AI product decisions without writing code.
objectives: Explain the difference between traditional software and machine learning in plain language
Describe how neural networks learn patterns from data and why data quality matters
Articulate how generative models and LLMs predict tokens to produce text
Distinguish training, fine-tuning, and inference and connect each to product cost and latency
Identify where AI fits well versus poorly in a product, and reason about failure modes like hallucination

quiz.q: What is the fundamental difference between traditional software and machine learning?
options: ML is always faster than traditional software
In ML, the system infers rules from examples instead of humans writing the rules
Traditional software can't run on the cloud
ML never makes mistakes
quiz.why: Traditional software relies on human-written rules, while ML learns patterns (rules) from example data, making its behavior probabilistic.

quiz.q: What is the core operation an LLM performs to generate text?
options: Looking up answers in a verified database
Predicting the next token based on prior context
Running if/then rules written by engineers
Searching the live internet for facts
quiz.why: LLMs generate output by repeatedly predicting the most likely next token given the preceding text—not by verifying facts.

quiz.q: Which process do your users trigger (and you pay for) every time they use an AI feature?
options: Training
Fine-tuning
Inference
Labeling
quiz.why: Inference is running the already-trained model to produce a result; it happens per request and drives ongoing cost and latency.

quiz.q: Which task is the BEST fit for an LLM-based feature?
options: Returning legally guaranteed exact figures with no human review
Drafting and summarizing content with human review
A safety system requiring strict determinism
Computing exact tax owed with no oversight
quiz.why: LLMs excel at fuzzy, pattern-rich tasks like drafting and summarizing, especially when paired with human review; guaranteed-correctness tasks are poor fits.

quiz.q: In one or two sentences, explain why LLMs hallucinate.
quiz.answer: LLMs predict statistically likely text rather than verified facts, so they produce fluent, plausible output that can be confidently wrong because they have no built-in notion of truth.
quiz.why: Hallucination stems from the next-token prediction objective optimizing for plausibility, not factual accuracy.

quiz.q: What does the 'context window' of an LLM refer to?
options: The model's training cost
How much text the model can consider at once (its working memory)
The number of users it can serve
The temperature setting
quiz.why: The context window is the amount of text the model can 'see' at one time, functioning like its working memory and limiting input length.

body_markdown:
## Why PMs Need a Mental Model (Not a PhD)

As an AI PM you won't train models yourself, but you will make decisions that depend on understanding *how* AI behaves: what it can do, where it breaks, what it costs, and why it sometimes confidently lies. This lesson gives you a durable, no-math mental model.

## Traditional Software vs. Machine Learning

Traditional software is **rules written by humans**: `if X then Y`. A developer specifies every behavior. It's predictable and auditable, but it can't handle messy, fuzzy problems (e.g., "is this photo a cat?").

Machine learning flips this. Instead of writing rules, you **show examples and let the system infer the rules**. You give it thousands of labeled cat/not-cat photos, and it learns the pattern. The output is a **model**—a learned function—not hand-written logic.

> Key shift: with ML you curate data and define objectives; the model discovers the rules. This makes behavior probabilistic, not deterministic.

## Neural Networks: Pattern Machines

A neural network is a stack of simple math units ("neurons") connected in layers. Each connection has a **weight**. During **training**, the model makes a guess, measures how wrong it was (the error), and nudges the weights to reduce that error—repeated millions of times. That nudging process is learning.

Mental model: imagine tuning thousands of knobs until the machine's outputs match the examples. "Deep learning" just means many layers of knobs, which lets the network capture very complex patterns.

- More data + bigger networks → can learn richer patterns
- Garbage data → garbage patterns (bias in, bias out)
- The model only knows what it has seen; it generalizes from training data

## Generative AI and LLMs: Predicting the Next Token

Large Language Models (LLMs) are neural networks trained on enormous amounts of text. Their core trick is shockingly simple: **predict the next chunk of text (a "token") given everything so far.** Do this repeatedly and you generate sentences, code, and answers.

Because they learned statistical patterns of language, they're great at fluent, plausible output—but they have no built-in notion of truth. They produce what is *likely*, not what is *verified*. This is why **hallucinations** (confident, wrong answers) happen.

- **Tokens**: text is split into pieces; pricing and limits are measured in tokens
- **Context window**: how much text the model can "see" at once (its working memory)
- **Prompt**: the input that steers the prediction
- **Temperature**: a knob for randomness/creativity vs. consistency

## Training vs. Fine-Tuning vs. Inference

- **Training**: the expensive, one-time-ish process of learning weights from massive data. Done by big labs; costs millions.
- **Fine-tuning**: taking a pretrained model and adjusting it on your narrower data/task. Cheaper, but still an investment.
- **Inference**: running the trained model to get an answer. This is what your users trigger every time—and what you pay for per request.

Product implication: most AI features ride on inference against an existing model (often via API). Latency and cost scale with tokens and model size. Bigger model = smarter but slower and pricier.

## Where AI Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Good fits:
- Fuzzy, pattern-rich tasks (summarizing, classifying, drafting, extracting)
- Tasks where "good enough" + human review is acceptable
- High-volume work that's tedious for humans

Poor fits:
- Tasks demanding guaranteed correctness with no oversight (e.g., exact legal/medical facts unaided)
- Problems with little or biased data
- Cases where explainability or strict determinism is legally required

## Failure Modes a PM Must Plan For

- **Hallucination**: fluent but false. Mitigate with grounding (retrieval), citations, and human-in-the-loop.
- **Bias**: reflects training data; test across user segments.
- **Drift / staleness**: model knowledge has a cutoff; the world changes.
- **Non-determinism**: same input can yield different outputs—affects testing and trust.

## The PM Takeaway

Think of an LLM as a brilliant, fast, well-read intern who is occasionally confidently wrong and never says "I don't know." Your product job is to set up the guardrails, context, and review loops that make that intern reliably useful.

slides.narration: Welcome. In this lesson we'll build a practical, no-math mental model of how modern AI actually works. You won't learn to code a model, but you'll be able to reason about AI products with confidence—understanding what these systems can do, where they fail, and why.

slides.title: Software vs. Machine Learning
bullets: Traditional software: humans write the rules (if X then Y)
Machine learning: show examples, the system infers the rules
Output is a learned 'model', not hand-written logic
Behavior becomes probabilistic, not deterministic
slides.narration: Start with the core shift. Traditional software is rules written by humans—predictable and auditable, but unable to handle fuzzy problems like recognizing a cat in a photo. Machine learning flips this: instead of writing rules, you show thousands of examples and let the system infer the pattern. The result is a learned model. The big consequence: AI behaves probabilistically, not deterministically.

slides.title: Neural Networks: Pattern Machines
bullets: Layers of simple units with adjustable 'weights'
Training = guess, measure error, nudge weights, repeat
'Deep' just means many layers of knobs
Garbage data in, garbage patterns out
slides.narration: Neural networks are stacks of simple math units connected by weighted links. Training is just guessing, measuring how wrong the guess was, and nudging the weights to do better—millions of times. Picture tuning thousands of knobs until outputs match the examples. Deep learning means many layers of those knobs. And remember: the model only knows what it's seen, so biased or poor data produces biased or poor results.

slides.title: Generative AI: Predicting the Next Token
bullets: LLMs trained on huge text to predict the next 'token'
Repeat prediction → sentences, code, answers
Fluent and plausible, but no built-in sense of truth
This is why hallucinations happen
slides.narration: Large language models do one core thing: predict the next chunk of text, called a token, given everything so far. Repeat that and you get full answers. Because they learned statistical patterns of language, they're excellent at producing fluent, plausible text. But they output what's likely, not what's verified—which is exactly why they hallucinate confident but wrong answers.

slides.title: Key LLM Vocabulary
bullets: Tokens: text pieces; pricing and limits are measured here
Context window: the model's working memory
Prompt: the input that steers the output
Temperature: randomness vs. consistency knob
slides.narration: A few terms you'll use daily. Tokens are the pieces text is split into—cost and length limits are measured in tokens. The context window is how much text the model can see at once, like working memory. The prompt is your steering input. And temperature controls how random or creative versus consistent the output is. Knowing these lets you talk precisely with your engineering team.

slides.title: Training, Fine-Tuning, Inference
bullets: Training: expensive, learns weights from massive data
Fine-tuning: adapt a pretrained model to your task
Inference: running the model per user request
Cost & latency scale with tokens and model size
slides.narration: Three processes to keep straight. Training is the massive, costly process of learning weights—done by big labs. Fine-tuning adapts an existing model to your narrower task, cheaper but still an investment. Inference is running the model to answer—what your users trigger and what you pay for every time. Most AI features just ride on inference via an API, and a bigger, smarter model means higher latency and cost.

slides.title: Where AI Fits—and Where It Doesn't
bullets: Great: summarizing, classifying, drafting, extracting
Great: high-volume tedious work with human review
Poor: guaranteed correctness with no oversight
Poor: little data, or strict explainability required
slides.narration: AI shines on fuzzy, pattern-rich tasks—summarizing, classifying, drafting, extracting—especially high-volume work where 'good enough plus human review' is fine. It struggles where you need guaranteed correctness without oversight, where data is scarce or biased, or where the law demands strict determinism and explainability. Matching the tool to the task is a core PM judgment call.

slides.title: Failure Modes to Design Around
bullets: Hallucination: ground with retrieval, citations, human review
Bias: test across user segments
Drift/staleness: knowledge has a cutoff date
Non-determinism: same input, different output
slides.narration: Plan for failure from day one. Hallucination is fluent falsehood—mitigate with grounding, citations, and humans in the loop. Bias reflects training data, so test across segments. Models go stale because their knowledge has a cutoff. And non-determinism means the same input can produce different outputs, which complicates testing and trust. Your guardrails are the product.

slides.title: The PM Takeaway
bullets: Think: brilliant, fast, well-read intern
...who is sometimes confidently wrong
...and rarely says 'I don't know'
Your job: context, guardrails, and review loops
slides.narration: Here's the mental model to carry with you. Treat an LLM like a brilliant, fast, well-read intern who is occasionally confidently wrong and almost never admits uncertainty. Your job as a PM is to build the context, guardrails, and review loops that turn that intern into something reliably useful. That's how you ship AI products responsibly.
